PAEDIATRIC__Fever in a Child:
Fever is the single commonest reason a child is brought to medical attention — a temperature ≥38°C. The whole task is to separate the vast majority with self-limiting viral illness from the few with life-threatening bacterial infection.
  • Use the NICE traffic-light system and the “sepsis” lens: assess colour, activity, respiratory, circulation / hydration and look for a focus.
  • The great red flags are a non-blanching rash (see non-blanching rash), meningism, a toxic / mottled child and prolonged capillary refill — think meningococcal disease and meningitis.
  • Age matters hugely: any fever under 3 months demands a full septic screen. Most children have viral exanthems, a urinary tract infection or a respiratory infection.
🚨A febrile child with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise. Give parenteral antibiotics without delay and activate the sepsis pathway (see meningococcal disease, sepsis). Fever under 3 months is high-risk — a temperature ≥38°C in an infant under 3 months mandates a full septic screen and admission; a fever ≥39°C at 3–6 months is an amber (intermediate-risk) feature on the NICE traffic-light system — assess carefully rather than screen every child automatically. Do not be reassured by a transient response to antipyretics. Consider Kawasaki disease in any child with fever for ≥5 days (see paediatric vasculitis), and always safeguard: an unusual presentation, delayed attendance or an inconsistent story raises child-protection concern.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Meningococcal sepsis
  • Fever + non-blanching / purpuric rash + unwell child (see non-blanching rash)
  • Cold mottled peripheries, prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia, drowsiness
  • → immediate parenteral antibiotics + fluids (see meningococcal disease)
🚩Serious bacterial infection / sepsis
  • NICE red features: mottled, grunting, tachypnoea, reduced consciousness, poor perfusion
  • Age <3 months with any fever → full septic screen (blood, urine, LP, CXR) (see sepsis)
  • Bacteraemia, pneumonia, pyelonephritis or bone / joint infection
🟠Meningitis / encephalitis
  • Fever + neck stiffness / photophobia; a bulging fontanelle in an infant
  • Non-specific in babies: irritability, poor feeding, high-pitched cry, drowsiness
  • → lumbar puncture and prompt antibiotics ± aciclovir (see meningitis / encephalitis)
🟠Focal / viral infection
  • Self-limiting viral exanthems, tonsillitis, otitis media (see childhood exanthems)
  • Respiratory: cough, coryza, tachypnoea, recession (see respiratory infection)
  • The commonest cause — but only after excluding the dangerous ones
🩹Urinary tract infection
  • Fever without an obvious focus, especially in infants (see paediatric urinary tract)
  • Offensive urine, vomiting, poor feeding, faltering growth
  • Always send a clean-catch urine in the febrile child with no focus
🩹Kawasaki disease
  • Fever ≥5 days + conjunctivitis, mucositis, rash, extremity change, node (see paediatric vasculitis)
  • Risk of coronary artery aneurysms → echocardiography
  • Treat with IVIG + aspirin to protect the coronaries
Traffic-light first, focus second. Grade every febrile child by colour, activity, respiratory and circulation, hunt actively for a non-blanching rash and meningism, and treat age <3 months as high-risk by default. Antipyretics treat discomfort, not risk.

At the bedside — the traffic-light features, the rash, the focus, the age

PAEDIATRIC__Rash in a Child:
A rash in a child is usually benign and viral, but a few patterns are life-threatening.
  • The first split is does it blanch? A non-blanching rash in an unwell, febrile child is meningococcal until proven otherwise — go straight to that focused pathway (see non-blanching rash).
  • Then characterise the morphology (maculopapular, vesicular, urticarial, purpuric), the distribution and evolution, and the company it keeps (fever, itch, systemic upset).
  • Most are self-limiting childhood exanthems — measles, rubella, roseola, slapped-cheek, chickenpox, hand-foot-and-mouth, scarlet fever. Common chronic rashes are atopic eczema and urticaria; bacterial causes include impetigo and cellulitis.
🚨Two rashes are emergencies: the non-blanching rash and urticaria with airway or circulatory compromise. A purpuric / non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal septicaemia — antibiotics now (see non-blanching rash, meningococcal disease). Urticaria with lip / tongue swelling, wheeze or hypotension is anaphylaxis — give IM adrenaline (see anaphylaxis). Beware evolving blistering / mucosal involvement or skin tenderness (Stevens–Johnson, staphylococcal scalded skin). And always safeguard: patterned bruising, cigarette-type burns or an inconsistent history demand child-protection assessment (see safeguarding).

  • Non-blanching petechiae or purpura + fever + unwell child (see non-blanching rash)
  • May start as a blanching macular rash — reassess and mark the skin
  • → immediate antibiotics + sepsis pathway (see meningococcal disease)

  • Urticaria + angioedema (lips, tongue) + wheeze / stridor / hypotension (see anaphylaxis)
  • Rapid onset after an allergen (food, drug, sting)
  • → IM adrenaline, ABC, remove the trigger
🟠Viral exanthems
  • Measles (Koplik spots, spreading maculopapular rash), rubella, roseola (see childhood exanthems)
  • Slapped-cheek (parvovirus B19), hand-foot-and-mouth, chickenpox (vesicles in crops)
  • Mostly self-limiting; notify measles and consider the immunosuppressed / pregnant contacts
🟠Atopic eczema
  • Itchy, dry, flexural rash in an atopic child (see atopic dermatitis)
  • Relapsing–remitting; watch for eczema herpeticum (painful, punched-out, unwell)
  • Emollients, topical steroids, treat flares and infection
🩹Bacterial skin infection
  • Impetigo (honey-crusted), cellulitis, scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue) (see skin infections)
  • Staphylococcal scalded skin — tender erythema, superficial peel in young children
  • Antibiotics; scarlet fever is a notifiable streptococcal illness
🩹Henoch–Schönlein purpura
  • Palpable purpura over buttocks / extensor legs + arthralgia + abdominal pain (see paediatric vasculitis)
  • Post-infectious IgA vasculitis; platelets are normal
  • Monitor renal involvement (urinalysis, BP); overlaps with the non-blanching rash pathway

PAEDIATRIC__Non-Blanching Rash:
A non-blanching rash is a red-flag sign that never blanches under pressure (the tumbler test) because blood has left the vessels.
  • This is the focused emergency lens of the broader picture — for the wider differential of childhood rashes see rash in a child. The overriding fear is meningococcal septicaemia in a febrile, unwell child (see meningococcal disease).
  • But a well child with a non-blanching rash has a different differential: HSP (palpable purpura, normal platelets) (see paediatric vasculitis) and ITP (isolated thrombocytopenia after a virus) (see immune thrombocytopenic purpura).
  • Do not miss the sinister ones — leukaemia (see paediatric cancers) and non-accidental injury (see safeguarding & child protection). Mechanical petechiae above the SVC (coughing, vomiting) are benign.
🚨A febrile child with a non-blanching rash has meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise — give parenteral antibiotics and treat for sepsis immediately. Do not wait for investigations (see meningococcal disease, sepsis). The rash may be petechial early and evolve to purpura; a spreading rash with cold peripheries signals shock and DIC (see disseminated intravascular coagulation). In the afebrile, well child, still exclude leukaemia (pallor, hepatosplenomegaly) and non-accidental injury — bruising or petechiae in a non-mobile infant is inflicted until proven otherwise (see safeguarding & child protection).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Meningococcal septicaemia
  • Fever + non-blanching purpura + toxic, mottled, shocked child (see meningococcal disease)
  • Rapidly spreading rash, cold peripheries, prolonged capillary refill
  • → immediate parenteral antibiotics + sepsis pathway (see sepsis)
🚩Non-accidental injury
  • Bruising / petechiae in a non-mobile infant — inflicted until proven otherwise (see safeguarding & child protection)
  • Patterned marks, unusual sites (ears, torso, buttocks), inconsistent or changing history
  • → safeguard, examine fully, clotting screen and skeletal survey
🟠Henoch–Schönlein purpura
  • Palpable purpura over extensor legs and buttocks (see paediatric vasculitis)
  • Arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain, IgA nephritis; often post-infectious
  • Platelets are normal — monitor BP and urinalysis for renal disease
🟠Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
  • Isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, often 1–2 weeks after a virus (see immune thrombocytopenic purpura)
  • Petechiae, bruising and mucosal bleeding with an otherwise normal blood count
  • Usually self-limiting; treat if significant bleeding
🩹Leukaemia
  • Petechiae / bruising + pallor, fatigue, fever, bone pain (see paediatric cancers)
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, other cytopenias on the count
  • → urgent FBC, blood film and marrow
🩹Mechanical / benign petechiae
  • Petechiae confined above the nipple line / SVC after forceful coughing, vomiting or crying
  • Well child, no systemic upset, normal blood count (see petechiae & purpura)
  • A diagnosis of exclusion once serious causes are ruled out
Fever changes everything. A febrile non-blanching rash is meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise; an afebrile, well child points to HSP, ITP or mechanical causes — but always exclude leukaemia and inflicted injury.

PAEDIATRIC__Limp in a Child:
A limp in a child is an abnormal gait from pain, weakness or deformity — and the differential is driven by age.
  • The must-not-miss is septic arthritis / osteomyelitis: a febrile child who refuses to weight-bear (see bone & joint infection, acute hot swollen joint). Other emergencies are malignancy (leukaemia, bone tumour) (see paediatric cancers) and non-accidental injury (see safeguarding & child protection).
  • Age frames the rest: an infant — DDH; a 3–10-year-old — transient synovitis or Perthes; an adolescent — SUFE (see paediatric orthopaedics). Persistent joint swelling suggests juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
  • Use Kocher’s criteria to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis.
🚨A febrile child who will not weight-bear has septic arthritis or osteomyelitis until proven otherwise — an orthopaedic emergency. Delay risks joint destruction and avascular necrosis; urgent joint aspiration and antibiotics are needed (see bone & joint infection). Never dismiss bone pain that wakes the child at night, pallor, bruising or weight loss — these suggest leukaemia or a bone tumour (see paediatric cancers). In the adolescent, missed SUFE causes permanent deformity — hip / knee pain with an externally rotated leg needs a frog-leg lateral X-ray. And a limp or fracture inconsistent with the history, or in a non-mobile child, demands safeguarding (see safeguarding).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Septic arthritis / osteomyelitis
  • Fever + refusal to weight-bear + a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint (see acute hot swollen joint)
  • Kocher criteria (fever, non-weight-bearing, raised ESR & WCC) predict septic arthritis
  • → urgent aspiration + IV antibiotics (see bone & joint infection)
🚩Malignancy
  • Bone pain waking at night, pallor, bruising, fever, weight loss (see paediatric cancers)
  • Leukaemia (marrow infiltration) or a primary bone tumour (osteosarcoma, Ewing)
  • → FBC, blood film and imaging
🟠Transient synovitis
  • Well child, 3–10 years, recent viral illness, able to weight-bear (see paediatric orthopaedics)
  • Afebrile or low-grade; normal / mildly raised inflammatory markers
  • A diagnosis of exclusion once septic arthritis is ruled out
🟠Slipped upper femoral epiphysis
  • Overweight adolescent, hip or referred knee pain, externally rotated leg (see paediatric orthopaedics)
  • Loss of internal rotation; may be acute or chronic
  • → frog-leg lateral X-ray; surgical pinning
🩹Developmental dysplasia of the hip
  • Infant / toddler: asymmetric skin creases, limited abduction, waddling gait (see paediatric orthopaedics)
  • Positive Barlow / Ortolani in the newborn; leg-length discrepancy
  • → ultrasound (<4.5 months) or X-ray
🩹Perthes / JIA
  • Perthes: boy 4–8y, insidious hip pain, limited internal rotation (avascular necrosis) (see paediatric orthopaedics)
  • JIA: joint swelling / stiffness >6 weeks, morning stiffness (see juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
  • X-ray both hips; refer for specialist management
Fever + non-weight-bearing = septic until proven otherwise. Apply Kocher’s criteria before labelling a limp “transient synovitis”, let age shape the differential, and always look for the systemic red flags of malignancy.

PAEDIATRIC__Vomiting in a Neonate / Infa:
Vomiting in a neonate or infant ranges from benign posseting to a surgical emergency — the colour and the company it keeps decide.
  • The one that must never be missed is bilious (green) vomiting, which is intestinal obstruction (malrotation with volvulus) until proven otherwise (see bilious vomiting, paediatric surgical GI).
  • Other emergencies are sepsis and necrotising enterocolitis (see sepsis, neonatal GI & abdominal wall), pyloric stenosis (projectile, 4–8 weeks) and intussusception (6 months–2 years) (see paediatric surgical GI), and raised intracranial pressure (see raised intracranial pressure).
  • Most infants simply have reflux / posseting — effortless, non-bilious, in a thriving baby.

Vomiting with a bulging fontanelle, drowsiness or an enlarging head is raised intracranial pressure. And in a preterm infant, bilious vomiting with distension and bloody stool is necrotising enterocolitis (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall).

PAEDIATRIC__Failure to Thrive:
Failure to thrive (faltering growth) is a sustained fall across weight centiles or a low growth velocity.
  • Frame the causes mechanistically: inadequate intake, inadequate absorption, increased requirement / losses, and non-organic / psychosocial factors — and always weigh safeguarding (see safeguarding & child protection).
  • Most cases are inadequate intake — feeding technique, volumes, poverty or reflux / feeding difficulty. Malabsorption points to coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis or cow’s-milk protein allergy; increased demand to congenital heart disease, chronic infection or malignancy.
  • Distinguish true faltering growth from the well child tracking a low but steady centile (constitutional / familial).
🚨Failure to thrive can be the first sign of neglect or of serious underlying disease — do not simply reassure. Weigh safeguarding in every case: disengagement, missed appointments, an inconsistent history or a flat, watchful child (see safeguarding & child protection). Do not miss cystic fibrosis (recurrent chest infections, steatorrhoea) (see cystic fibrosis), congenital heart disease (breathless / sweaty on feeds, murmur) (see congenital heart disease) or malignancy (mass, pallor, systemic upset) (see paediatric cancers). Faltering growth with loss of acquired skills is a red flag for a metabolic or neurodegenerative disorder (see developmental regression).

PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Regression:
Developmental regression is the loss of previously acquired skills — and it is always a red flag.
  • This is distinct from developmental delay (skills not yet reached) (see developmental delay): regression means a child could do something and now cannot.
  • The sinister causes are neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders (leukodystrophies, storage disorders, mitochondrial disease) (see genetic syndromes), acquired brain injury — encephalitis, a brain tumour or inflicted head injury — and epileptic encephalopathies (West syndrome, Landau–Kleffner) (see paediatric seizures).
  • Treatable mimics — hypothyroidism (see hypothyroidism) — must be excluded, and autistic regression (loss of language / social skills at 18–24 months) (see neurodevelopmental & behavioural) recognised.
🚨Loss of acquired skills is never normal — it mandates urgent investigation. An acute regression with fever, seizures or reduced consciousness is encephalitis or raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise (see meningitis / encephalitis, raised intracranial pressure). Progressive loss of vision, motor and cognitive skills suggests a neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder needing metabolic screening and MRI (see genetic syndromes). Always exclude treatable causes — hypothyroidism and seizures — and safeguard: regression with unexplained injuries or an inconsistent history raises non-accidental injury (see safeguarding & child protection).

PAEDIATRIC__Stridor in a Child:
Stridor is a harsh, monophonic noise of upper-airway obstruction — usually inspiratory.
  • The task is to spot the child whose airway is about to close and separate them from the many with benign viral croup (see stridor & upper airway).
  • The great emergencies are epiglottitis / bacterial tracheitis (toxic, drooling, tripod), an inhaled foreign body (sudden choking) and anaphylaxis (see anaphylaxis).
  • The commonest cause is croup (barking cough, coryza, 6 months–6 years, peak 6 months–3 years); chronic stridor from birth in a thriving baby is usually laryngomalacia (see stridor & upper airway). The cardinal rule: in a child with possible epiglottitis, keep them calm and do not examine the throat.
🚨Do not distress a child with severe stridor — agitation and throat examination can precipitate complete airway obstruction. Suspect epiglottitis in a toxic, drooling child sitting forward with a muffled voice and no cough — call senior anaesthetic / ENT help and secure the airway in a controlled setting (see stridor & upper airway). Sudden stridor with a choking episode is an inhaled foreign body; stridor with urticaria, facial swelling and wheeze is anaphylaxis needing IM adrenaline (see anaphylaxis). Give oxygen and nebulised adrenaline for critical obstruction while help is mobilised, and keep the child on the parent’s lap.

PAEDIATRIC__Wheeze in a Child:
Wheeze is a high-pitched, usually expiratory, polyphonic noise of lower-airway obstruction. Age and pattern drive the diagnosis.
  • Under one year, an acute first wheeze with coryza and crackles is usually bronchiolitis (see lower respiratory infection & wheeze); in older, atopic children episodic wheeze with triggers is asthma or viral-induced wheeze (see asthma).
  • The emergencies are life-threatening asthma (silent chest, exhaustion, SpO₂ <92%), anaphylaxis (see anaphylaxis) and an inhaled foreign body (sudden onset, focal) (see stridor & upper airway).
  • Recurrent wet cough with faltering growth suggests cystic fibrosis (see cystic fibrosis); rarely, wheeze reflects cardiac failure (see congenital heart disease).
🚨A silent chest, exhaustion or SpO₂ below 92% signals life-threatening asthma — the wheeze can disappear as air entry fails. Treat immediately with oxygen, back-to-back bronchodilators and steroids, and call for senior help (see asthma). Wheeze with urticaria, facial swelling or hypotension after an allergen is anaphylaxis — give IM adrenaline (see anaphylaxis). Consider an inhaled foreign body when wheeze starts suddenly after a choking episode or is focal / unilateral (see stridor & upper airway). Do not label every wheezy infant “asthma”: bronchiolitis and viral-induced wheeze in the very young often do not respond to bronchodilators.

PAEDIATRIC__The Floppy Infant:
The floppy infant has reduced muscle tone (hypotonia) — a rag-doll baby who slips through your hands, with head lag and a frog-leg posture (see reduced tone).
  • The first, vital split is central vs peripheral: central hypotonia (brain) comes with reduced alertness and preserved / brisk reflexes; peripheral hypotonia (anterior horn cell → muscle) shows an alert baby with weakness and reduced reflexes.
  • The emergencies are sepsis / meningitis (acute floppiness) (see sepsis) and spinal muscular atrophy (see neuromuscular disorders).
  • Central causes include hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (see neonatal medicine), Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome and evolving cerebral palsy.
🚨An acutely floppy infant who is unwell has sepsis or meningitis until proven otherwise — screen and treat immediately. Floppiness with poor feeding, temperature instability or apnoea is a medical emergency (see sepsis, meningitis). Do not miss spinal muscular atrophy (type 1): a progressively weak, areflexic but alert baby with tongue fasciculations and a bell-shaped chest — disease-modifying therapy is time-critical (see neuromuscular disorders). Congenital hypothyroidism (prolonged jaundice, constipation, coarse features) is a treatable cause — check the newborn screen (see hypothyroidism). And always safeguard: floppiness with unexplained injury raises inflicted head injury (see safeguarding).

PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Jaundice:
Neonatal jaundice is yellow discolouration from raised bilirubin — and timing is everything.
  • Jaundice within 24 hours of birth is always pathological: haemolysis (rhesus / ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency) or congenital infection / sepsis until proven otherwise (see neonatal medicine, sepsis).
  • Jaundice at day 2–14 in a well term baby is usually physiological or breast-milk jaundice (unconjugated) (see neonatal medicine).
  • Prolonged jaundice (>14 days term, >21 preterm) must be split into unconjugated (hypothyroidism, breast milk, UTI) and conjugated — the last raises biliary atresia, where pale stools and dark urine demand urgent action (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall). Very high unconjugated bilirubin threatens kernicterus (see jaundice).
🚨Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological — measure bilirubin urgently and treat. The great fears are haemolysis, sepsis (any jaundiced, unwell baby) and kernicterus — acute bilirubin encephalopathy from very high unconjugated levels, presenting with lethargy, a high-pitched cry, hypertonia and arching, and causing permanent brain injury (see neonatal medicine, sepsis). Plot bilirubin on the treatment threshold chart and start phototherapy or exchange transfusion promptly. Prolonged conjugated jaundice with pale stools and dark urine is biliary atresia — the Kasai portoenterostomy must be done early (ideally <60 days) for a good outcome (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall).

PAEDIATRIC__Seizures & Funny Turns in Ch:
“Funny turns” in children span true epileptic seizures and a host of non-epileptic paroxysmal events — and the eye-witness account decides more than any test (see seizures, transient loss of consciousness).
  • The emergencies are meningitis / encephalitis (seizure + fever + unwell) (see meningitis / encephalitis), hypoglycaemia, status epilepticus and raised intracranial pressure.
  • The commonest benign event is the febrile convulsion (6 months–5 years, brief, generalised, with fever) (see febrile convulsion); recurrent unprovoked seizures are epilepsy (see paediatric seizures).
  • Non-epileptic mimics — vasovagal syncope, reflex anoxic seizures and breath-holding spells — are benign but need recognising, and every case is safeguarded (see safeguarding & child protection).
🚨A seizure with fever and an unwell child is meningitis or encephalitis until proven otherwise, and any seizing child needs a bedside glucose. Do not assume a febrile convulsion in a drowsy, toxic or focal child (see meningitis / encephalitis). Check glucose immediately — hypoglycaemia is a rapidly reversible cause. A seizure lasting >5 minutes is status epilepticus — follow the APLS algorithm with benzodiazepines (see epilepsy). Early-morning headache and vomiting with seizures suggests raised intracranial pressure / tumour (see raised intracranial pressure). And an unexplained seizure or apnoea in an infant, with retinal haemorrhages, is inflicted head injury (see safeguarding & child protection).

PAEDIATRIC__Constipation in a Child:
Constipation in a child is usually functional (idiopathic) — the great majority — but a handful of red flags signal serious organic disease.
  • Most children present with infrequent, hard, painful stools, a withholding cycle and overflow soiling, and respond to disimpaction, maintenance laxatives and behavioural measures.
  • The must-not-miss is Hirschsprung’s disease — suspect it whenever there is delayed passage of meconium (>48 hours), symptoms from birth, abdominal distension or ribbon stools (see paediatric surgical GI).

Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting and an empty rectum with explosive stool on withdrawal of the examining finger demand a suction rectal biopsy (see paediatric surgical GI). Do not miss red-flag features: onset in the first weeks of life, ribbon stools, faltering growth, abnormal sacrum or lower-limb neurology (spinal cord lesion), a distended abdomen or perianal signs of trauma. Faltering growth, poor hygiene or an inconsistent story raise neglect (see safeguarding & child protection). Reserve the label “functional” for the well, thriving child with a typical history.

PAEDIATRIC__Safeguarding:
Safeguarding is the presentation of a child whose features raise concern for abuse or neglect.
  • Every clinician has a duty to recognise, document and act (see safeguarding & child protection).
  • The forms are physical abuse (patterned or inconsistent bruising, injuries incompatible with the developmental stage, delayed presentation), neglect and non-organic failure to thrive (see failure to thrive), emotional abuse, sexual abuse (anogenital signs, a sexually transmitted infection, sexualised behaviour or a disclosure) and fabricated or induced illness.
  • The single most specific alarm is bruising, a fracture or an intracranial injury in a non-mobile infant — inflicted until proven otherwise. Always weigh medical mimics such as a bleeding disorder (see bruising & bleeding); the same safeguarding duty extends to vulnerable adults (see adult safeguarding).
🚨Bruising, fractures or intracranial injury in a non-mobile infant is inflicted until proven otherwise — a child-protection emergency. Escalate to a senior and the safeguarding lead, examine and document fully, and admit to a place of safety (see safeguarding & child protection). Red flags across every presentation are an injury incompatible with the history or developmental stage, a changing or inconsistent account, delayed presentation, and multiple injuries of different ages. Suspect abusive head trauma in an infant with encephalopathy, apnoea or seizures and retinal haemorrhages, and fabricated or induced illness when persistent unexplained symptoms do not fit the tests. Never confront — document verbatim, preserve evidence and follow local child-protection procedures.

PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Respiratory Distres:
Neonatal respiratory distress is the newborn with tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, recession and cyanosis — the commonest reason a baby is admitted to the neonatal unit. Think in timelines and risk factors.
  • Prematurity points to respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency, ground-glass on X-ray) (see neonatal medicine); a term baby after caesarean with mild, rapidly resolving distress has transient tachypnoea of the newborn; meconium-stained liquor suggests meconium aspiration.
  • Always exclude sepsis / congenital pneumonia (grunting, temperature instability; group B streptococcus) (see sepsis).
  • Do not miss surgical and cardiac causes — congenital diaphragmatic hernia (see paediatric surgical GI), congenital heart disease (see congenital heart disease) and oesophageal atresia / tracheo-oesophageal fistula; central cyanosis needs the blue-baby pathway.
🚨Treat every distressed newborn as possible sepsis and rule out a surgical or duct-dependent cardiac cause. Give respiratory support and antibiotics after cultures if sepsis is possible (see sepsis, neonatal medicine). A scaphoid abdomen with a displaced apex and poor air entry is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia — do not bag-mask ventilate; intubate and pass a large nasogastric tube (see paediatric surgical GI). Central cyanosis that fails the hyperoxia test is duct-dependent heart disease needing prostaglandin E (see neonatal cyanosis). Sudden deterioration with asymmetric chest signs is a pneumothorax. A baby who chokes and cyanoses with feeds and cannot pass a nasogastric tube has oesophageal atresia.

PAEDIATRIC__Bilious Vomiting (Neonate):
Bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.
  • Bile below the ampulla means intestinal obstruction — the fear is malrotation with midgut volvulus, where the whole midgut twists on a narrow mesentery and infarcts within hours (see paediatric surgical GI).   • Any green vomit demands urgent surgical review.
🚨Green bilious vomiting in a previously well neonate is malrotation with volvulus until excluded — a time-critical emergency. Delay of hours risks irreversible midgut infarction; resuscitate, keep nil by mouth, pass a nasogastric tube and arrange an urgent upper GI contrast study and surgical review (see paediatric surgical GI). In the preterm baby, bilious aspirates with abdominal distension, bloody stool and a tense abdomen are necrotising enterocolitis (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall). A shocked, distended baby may be septic (see sepsis). Do not attribute green vomit to reflux or feeding — obstruction must be actively excluded first.

🚩Malrotation with midgut volvulus
  • Green bilious vomiting in a previously well neonate, sudden, may become shocked (see paediatric surgical GI)
  • Corkscrew / abnormal duodenojejunal flexure on upper GI contrast; time-critical midgut ischaemia
  • → resuscitate, NG tube, nil by mouth, emergency laparotomy (Ladd procedure)
🚩Necrotising enterocolitis
  • Preterm baby: bilious aspirates, distension, bloody stool, tense abdomen (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall)
  • Pneumatosis intestinalis on X-ray; systemic deterioration and shock
  • → nil by mouth, NG decompression, antibiotics, surgery if perforation
🟠Intestinal atresia / obstruction
  • Duodenal atresia — “double bubble”, associated with Down’s syndrome (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall)
  • Jejunoileal atresia — multiple dilated loops, bilious vomiting from birth
  • → abdominal X-ray; surgical correction
🟠Hirschsprung’s disease
  • Delayed meconium >48h + distension + bilious vomiting (see paediatric surgical GI)
  • Empty rectum with explosive stool on PR; risk of enterocolitis
  • → contrast enema and suction rectal biopsy
🩹Meconium ileus (cystic fibrosis)
  • Failure to pass meconium + distension + bilious vomiting; family history of CF (see cystic fibrosis)
  • Inspissated meconium; “soap-bubble” appearance; microcolon on contrast
  • → contrast enema (may be therapeutic); confirm and treat CF
🩹Sepsis / medical mimics
  • Shocked, distended, lethargic baby — sepsis with ileus (see sepsis)
  • Non-bilious / milky vomit has a different differential (see vomiting in a neonate / infant)
  • → cultures, antibiotics and resuscitation; keep surgery involved
Green means surgeon. Any bilious vomiting in a neonate is obstruction until excluded — and the time-critical diagnosis is malrotation with volvulus. Resuscitate, decompress and get an urgent upper GI contrast study; do not wait to see if it settles.

PAEDIATRIC__Neonatal Cyanosis (Blue Baby:
A blue baby is a neonate with cyanosis — and the first task is to separate central from peripheral.
  • Central cyanosis (blue tongue and mucous membranes, <85–90% saturations) is always pathological; peripheral cyanosis (blue hands and feet with a pink tongue) in the first days is usually benign acrocyanosis.
  • The overriding fear is duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease (see congenital heart disease) — transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary / tricuspid atresia (total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage is cyanotic but not duct-dependent).
  • The hyperoxia test separates cardiac from respiratory disease (see neonatal respiratory distress), and a failed test needs prostaglandin E to keep the duct open. Also weigh persistent pulmonary hypertension, sepsis (see sepsis) and the general cyanosis lens.
🚨Central cyanosis that does not correct with high-flow oxygen (a failed hyperoxia test) is duct-dependent congenital heart disease until proven otherwise — start prostaglandin E and get an urgent echocardiogram. Do not wait (see congenital heart disease). Measure pre- and post-ductal saturations and feel the femoral pulses (weak / absent in coarctation). A shocked, mottled, poorly perfused baby may be septic or have a closing duct — treat both (see sepsis). Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn gives labile, marked cyanosis, often after meconium aspiration or asphyxia. Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen with chocolate-brown blood is methaemoglobinaemia. Never dismiss central cyanosis as “just the cold”.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Duct-dependent cyanotic CHD
  • Central cyanosis + failed hyperoxia test, often no murmur; single second heart sound (see congenital heart disease)
  • Transposition, tetralogy, pulmonary / tricuspid atresia; decompensate as the duct closes (TAPVD is cyanotic but not duct-dependent)
  • → prostaglandin E to keep the duct open, urgent echocardiography and cardiology
🚩Sepsis / cardiovascular collapse
  • Cyanosis + shock, mottling, temperature instability and poor perfusion (see sepsis)
  • Cannot reliably distinguish from a closing duct at the bedside — cover both
  • → cultures, antibiotics, fluids and respiratory support without delay
🟠Respiratory causes
  • Grunting, recession, tachypnoea with an abnormal chest X-ray (see neonatal respiratory distress)
  • RDS (preterm), TTN (term caesarean), meconium aspiration, pneumonia
  • → the hyperoxia test improves the saturations; respiratory support
🟠Persistent pulmonary hypertension (PPHN)
  • Labile, marked cyanosis with a large pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient
  • Follows meconium aspiration, asphyxia or sepsis; right-to-left shunt across the duct
  • → echocardiography, oxygenation, inhaled nitric oxide
🩹Peripheral cyanosis / acrocyanosis
  • Blue hands and feet with a pink tongue in a well baby in the first days
  • Benign vasomotor instability; central saturations are normal
  • → reassurance once central cyanosis is excluded
🩹Methaemoglobinaemia & other
  • Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen with chocolate-brown blood
  • Congenital or acquired; also polycythaemia and hypothermia mimic cyanosis
  • → co-oximetry; methylene blue if methaemoglobinaemia
Central or peripheral, then hyperoxia. A blue tongue is central cyanosis and always pathological; blue extremities with a pink tongue are benign acrocyanosis. In central cyanosis, a failed hyperoxia test means duct-dependent heart disease — prostaglandin E — while an improving test points to a respiratory cause.

PAEDIATRIC__Dysmorphic Features / Suspec:
Dysmorphic features are unusual physical characteristics that, in a recognisable pattern, suggest an underlying genetic syndrome.
  • The clinical task is not only to name the syndrome but to screen for the anomalies it carries.
  • Group the causes: chromosomal — Down (trisomy 21), Edwards (18), Patau (13) and Turner (45,X) (see chromosomal disorders); single-gene / microdeletion — Noonan, Williams, DiGeorge (22q11), Prader-Willi and fragile X (see genetic syndromes); and teratogenic — fetal alcohol syndrome.
  • Many carry congenital heart disease (see congenital heart disease) and other structural anomalies, and most are associated with developmental delay (see developmental delay) and learning disability (see learning disability). A three-generation family history and a full anomaly screen guide testing.
🚨The danger of a dysmorphic syndrome is its associated anomalies — screen every child actively. A number carry duct-dependent or complex congenital heart disease that decompensates in the newborn (see congenital heart disease), and Down syndrome is associated with duodenal atresia presenting as bilious vomiting (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall). Trisomy 18 and 13 carry multiple severe anomalies and a poor prognosis — involve senior and palliative teams early. DiGeorge (22q11) causes hypocalcaemia (seizures), cardiac outflow defects and immunodeficiency. Do not label a child dysmorphic without parental features, ethnicity and gestational age in mind, and always refer to clinical genetics for counselling and definitive testing.

  • Multiple severe malformations and a poor prognosis (see chromosomal disorders)
  • Edwards: rocker-bottom feet, clenched overlapping fingers, micrognathia; Patau: cleft, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly
  • → confirm karyotype; involve senior and palliative teams early
🟠Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
  • Hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, flat occiput, protruding tongue (see chromosomal disorders)
  • Associated: CHD (AVSD), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, leukaemia, hearing loss
  • → karyotype / QF-PCR; echo, screening and MDT follow-up
🟠Turner syndrome (45,X)
  • Female: webbed neck, lymphoedema, widely spaced nipples, short stature (see chromosomal disorders)
  • Associated: coarctation / bicuspid aortic valve, ovarian failure, renal anomalies
  • → karyotype; echo, renal USS and endocrine follow-up
🩹Microdeletion / single-gene syndromes
  • Noonan (webbed neck, pulmonary stenosis, normal karyotype), Williams (supravalvular AS, sociable) (see genetic syndromes)
  • DiGeorge / 22q11 (hypocalcaemia, cardiac outflow, immunodeficiency), Prader-Willi, fragile X
  • → microarray / targeted gene testing; clinical genetics referral
🩹Teratogenic / non-syndromic
  • Fetal alcohol syndrome: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, small palpebral fissures, growth restriction
  • Deformations / positional features and benign familial variants
  • → correlate with the pregnancy and family history
Recognise the pattern, then screen the anomalies. Group by chromosomal, single-gene / microdeletion and teratogenic causes, confirm with the right genetic test, and actively look for the cardiac, GI, renal, endocrine, hearing and vision problems the syndrome carries.

PAEDIATRIC__Abdominal Mass in a Child:
An abdominal mass in a child is malignancy until proven otherwise, though many masses are benign.
  • The two must-not-miss tumours are Wilms’ tumour (nephroblastoma) — a smooth flank mass that does not cross the midline in a 1–5-year-old — and neuroblastoma — an irregular mass that crosses the midline in an often unwell child (see paediatric cancers). Hepatoblastoma gives firm hepatomegaly with a raised AFP.
  • Benign causes are common: the faecal mass of constipation (see constipation), an enlarged / ballotable kidney from hydronephrosis or a multicystic dysplastic kidney (see paediatric urinary tract), a full bladder, and the sausage-shaped mass of intussusception (see paediatric surgical GI).
  • Use the site, mobility and the child’s wellbeing to triage, and see the general abdominal mass lens.
🚨A firm, painless abdominal mass in a young child needs urgent imaging and a very urgent referral (for an appointment within 48 hours) for suspected cancer — do not palpate a Wilms’ tumour repeatedly. Suspect malignancy with weight loss, pallor, night sweats or a hard mass (see paediatric cancers). Neuroblastoma may present with a mass crossing the midline, hypertension, bone pain, periorbital bruising and metastases. Wilms’ gives haematuria and hypertension; avoid vigorous or repeated palpation. A tender sausage-shaped mass with redcurrant-jelly stool is intussusception — a surgical emergency (see paediatric surgical GI). Always exclude the simple explanations first — a loaded colon or a full bladder — but never assume them without excluding a tumour.

  • Firm hepatomegaly with a markedly raised AFP in a young child (see paediatric cancers)

  • Enlarged, ballotable kidney(s), often bilateral if polycystic (see enlarged / ballotable kidneys)

  • Palpable, mobile, indentable mass along the colon with hard stool (see constipation)

  • Sausage-shaped mass + colicky pain + redcurrant-jelly stool, 3 months–2 years (see paediatric surgical GI)

  • → ultrasound (target sign); air / contrast enema reduction

PAEDIATRIC__Leukocoria / Absent Red Refl:
Leukocoria is a white pupillary reflex — an absent or abnormal red reflex — and it is a sight- and life-threatening sign until proven otherwise.
  • The red reflex is checked at every newborn and 6-week examination; any white, asymmetric or absent reflex needs same-week ophthalmology referral.
  • The must-not-miss diagnosis is retinoblastoma, the commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood, which also presents with a new squint (see paediatric cancers).
  • Common non-malignant causes are congenital cataract, which needs early surgery to prevent deprivation amblyopia (see cataracts), and retinopathy of prematurity in preterm, low-birth-weight babies (see neonatal medicine). Other retinal causes include Coats disease and persistent fetal vasculature; a syndromic child needs a wider work-up (see suspected syndrome).
🚨Leukocoria is retinoblastoma until an ophthalmologist proves otherwise — refer urgently, never “watch and wait”. Retinoblastoma threatens both sight and life, and is curable when caught early (see paediatric cancers). A white reflex noticed by a parent, seen on flash photographs, or a new squint, are classic presentations. Any absent or asymmetric red reflex at the newborn or 6-week check mandates same-week ophthalmology review. A dense congenital cataract must be operated on within the first weeks of life to prevent irreversible deprivation amblyopia (see cataracts). A bilateral or familial white reflex raises hereditary retinoblastoma — screen siblings and refer for genetic testing.

PAEDIATRIC__Developmental Delay:
Developmental delay is failure to reach milestones at the expected age — and the first split is global versus domain-specific.
  • Global developmental delay is significant delay in two or more of the domains (gross motor, fine motor / vision, speech / language / hearing, social) (see neurodevelopmental & behavioural); isolated delay affects one domain.
  • This is distinct from developmental regression — the loss of previously acquired skills, which is a red flag for neurodegenerative or metabolic disease (see developmental regression).
  • Look hard for treatable and serious causes: congenital hypothyroidism (see hypothyroidism), hearing or visual impairment (see hearing loss), cerebral palsy (see cerebral palsy), genetic / chromosomal syndromes (see genetic syndromes), Duchenne muscular dystrophy (see neuromuscular disorders) and neglect.
🚨Regression — the loss of skills already gained — is a neurological red flag and must be separated from delay. Loss of skills points to neurodegenerative, metabolic or structural disease and needs urgent investigation (see developmental regression). Do not miss the treatable causes: screen hearing and vision in every child with speech or global delay, check thyroid function (congenital hypothyroidism is on the newborn screen but can be missed) (see hypothyroidism), and consider neglect and safeguarding. A boy with gross-motor delay, calf pseudohypertrophy and a positive Gower’s sign has Duchenne muscular dystrophy — check the creatine kinase (see neuromuscular disorders). Loss of head control, hand preference before one year, or abnormal tone (key red-flag limit ages: not sitting unsupported by 9 months, not walking by 18 months, no words by 18 months, no 2-word phrases by 2½ years) suggests cerebral palsy.

PAEDIATRIC__Behavioural / Neurodevelopme:
Behavioural and neurodevelopmental concerns cover the child brought with inattention, hyperactivity, or social and communication difficulties.
  • The two headline diagnoses are ADHD — developmentally inappropriate inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity present in two or more settings before age 12 — and autism spectrum disorder — persistent difficulties in social communication with restricted, repetitive behaviours and sensory sensitivities (see neurodevelopmental & behavioural).
  • Both are clinical, multi-informant diagnoses that require screening for comorbidity (learning disability, anxiety / mood, epilepsy, sleep) and for safeguarding (see safeguarding).
  • Always consider differentials and mimics — hearing loss (see hearing loss), absence seizures and global developmental delay (see developmental delay) — and syndromic causes such as fragile X (see genetic syndromes).
🚨Behavioural change is not always “just behaviour” — screen for safeguarding, risk and a medical mimic. A sudden change, fearfulness or regression can signal abuse or neglect (see safeguarding). Neurodevelopmental disorders carry a high burden of comorbidity and risk — depression, self-harm (see self-harm & suicidal ideation), anxiety and epilepsy. Do not diagnose ADHD or ASD without excluding hearing loss (see hearing loss) and absence seizures (staring spells mistaken for inattention) (see paediatric seizures). Diagnosis is multi-setting and multidisciplinary, never from a single clinic snapshot — gather information from home and school.

PAEDIATRIC__Poor Feeding / Unwell Neonat:
Poor feeding is often the first and only sign that a neonate is seriously unwell — treat it as a red flag, not a feeding technique problem.
  • The overriding fear is sepsis (early- or late-onset, group B streptococcus): poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability and poor perfusion (see sepsis).
  • Do not miss duct-dependent congenital heart disease, which collapses as the arterial duct closes (see congenital heart disease), an inborn error of metabolism (vomiting, lethargy, acidosis, hypoglycaemia) (see neonatal medicine), and surgical GI disease such as necrotising enterocolitis (see neonatal GI & abdominal wall).
  • Neurological causes overlap with the floppy infant. Genuine feeding difficulty (prematurity, cleft, reflux, technique) is a diagnosis of exclusion (see infant feeding & reflux).
🚨Assume the poorly feeding neonate is septic until proven otherwise — a full septic screen and antibiotics come first. Signs are non-specific; a low threshold saves lives (see sepsis). Always check a bedside glucose — hypoglycaemia is common and rapidly reversible. A baby who collapses, becomes cyanosed or loses femoral pulses in the first days has duct-dependent heart disease needing prostaglandin E (see congenital heart disease). Persistent vomiting with lethargy, acidosis or hyperammonaemia is an inborn error of metabolism (see neonatal medicine). Bilious vomiting with distension is surgical (see bilious vomiting). Never discharge a genuinely poorly feeding baby.

PAEDIATRIC__Bedwetting / Enuresis:
Enuresis is involuntary wetting in a child old enough to be dry (nocturnal after around 5 years), and the key split is primary versus secondary.
  • Primary enuresis (never been reliably dry) is usually benign and developmental; secondary enuresis (wetting after ≥6 months of dryness) is more concerning and demands a cause.
  • The red flags to exclude are new-onset type 1 diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) (see type 1 diabetes), a urinary tract infection (see paediatric urinary tract), constipation (a loaded rectum compresses the bladder) (see constipation in a child), and emotional distress or safeguarding (see safeguarding & child protection).
  • Daytime symptoms, straining or a poor stream suggest a structural or neurological cause (see polyuria & polydipsia).
🚨Secondary enuresis with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss is new type 1 diabetes — check a glucose and ketones the same day. Do not miss the child slipping into diabetic ketoacidosis (see type 1 diabetes). Screen for a urinary tract infection (dysuria, daytime frequency, offensive urine) (see paediatric urinary tract) and for constipation, which is a common and treatable cause — treat the bowel first (see constipation in a child). New secondary bedwetting can signal emotional distress, bullying or abuse (see safeguarding & child protection). Daytime wetting with straining, a poor stream, dribbling or abnormal lower-limb neurology / a sacral dimple suggests posterior urethral valves, an ectopic ureter or spinal dysraphism — not simple enuresis.

  • A loaded rectum compresses the bladder → daytime and night-time wetting (see constipation in a child)
